$$\text{A primitive root mod } n \text{ is an integer } g \text{ such that}$$

$$\{g^1,g^2,\ldots,g^{\phi(n)}\} \pmod n \text{ generates all integers coprime to } n$$

$$\text{Equivalently, the smallest } k \text{ with } g^k\equiv1\pmod n \text{ is } k=\phi(n)$$

$$\text{Example: } n=7, \ \phi(7)=6, \ \text{test } g=3$$

$$3^1=3,\ 3^2=2,\ 3^3=6,\ 3^4=4,\ 3^5=5,\ 3^6=1 \pmod7$$

$$\{3,2,6,4,5,1\} = \{1,2,3,4,5,6\} \implies 3 \text{ is a primitive root mod } 7$$

$$n \text{ has a primitive root if and only if } n \in \{1,\ 2,\ 4,\ p^k,\ 2p^k\}$$

$$\text{where } p \text{ is an odd prime and } k \geq 1$$

$$\text{Number of primitive roots mod } n = \phi(\phi(n))$$

$$\text{Example: } n=7, \ \phi(7)=6, \ \phi(6)=\phi(2)\phi(3)=1\times2=2$$

$$\text{So there are 2 primitive roots mod 7: } g=3 \text{ and } g=5$$

## Bezout's Identity
For integers a, b with gcd(a,b)=d, there exist integers x, y such that
$$ax+by=d$$
d = smallest positive value ax+by can take. Every value ax+by is a multiple of d, and every multiple of d is achievable.

> Special case, a,b coprime (gcd=1): ax+by=1 has integer solutions

## Linear Congruence
ax = b (mod n): let d=gcd(a,n). Solvable iff d divides b.

| condition | result |
|---|---|
| d does not divide b | no solution |
| d divides b | exactly d distinct solutions mod n |

**Find x,y** (or solve congruence): use Extended Euclidean Algorithm

**Application**: modular inverse of a mod n exists iff gcd(a,n)=1, found via x in ax+ny=1

## Solving ax ≡ b (mod n)
Let d = gcd(a,n).

**Case d=1**: divide directly by a (using modular inverse)
$$2x \equiv 4 \pmod 7$$
gcd(2,7)=1, so divide both sides by 2 directly: x ≡ 2 (mod 7)

**Case d>1**: if d divides b, divide both sides AND the modulus by d
$$2x \equiv 4 \pmod 6$$
gcd(2,6)=2, divide everything (both sides and modulus) by 2: x ≡ 2 (mod 3)
This gives d=2 distinct solutions mod 6: x ≡ 2 or x ≡ 5 (mod 6)

> If d does not divide b, no solution exists at all

Chicken McNugget Theorem (Frobenius, 2 coprime coins): for coprime $a, b$
$$\text{largest non-representable value} = ab-a-b$$
$$\text{count of non-representable positive integers} = \frac{(a-1)(b-1)}{2}$$

Example: $a=6, b=11$ (coprime)
$$\text{Frobenius number} = 6\times11-6-11 = 49$$
$$\text{non-representable count} = \frac{5\times10}{2}=25$$

problems.questionText:
$$\textbf{Question}$$

$$\text{Let } n \text{ be the least positive integer for which } 149^n-2^n \text{ is divisible by } 3^3\cdot5^5\cdot7^7.$$

$$\text{Find the number of positive integer divisors of } n.$$
problems.solutionText:
$$\textbf{Solution}$$

$$\text{By LTE: } \nu_3(149^n-2^n) = \nu_3(147)+\nu_3(n) = 1+\nu_3(n)$$

$$1+\nu_3(n)\geq3 \implies \nu_3(n)\geq2 \implies 3^2\mid n$$

$$\text{By LTE: } \nu_7(149^n-2^n) = \nu_7(147)+\nu_7(n) = 2+\nu_7(n)$$

$$2+\nu_7(n)\geq7 \implies \nu_7(n)\geq5 \implies 7^5\mid n$$

$$\text{For 5: } 149^n\equiv2^n\pmod5 \text{ requires } 4\mid n. \text{ Let } n=4c.$$

$$\nu_5(149^{4c}-2^{4c}) = \nu_5(149^4-16)+\nu_5(c) = 1+\nu_5(c)$$

$$1+\nu_5(c)\geq5 \implies \nu_5(c)\geq4 \implies 5^4\mid c \implies 4\cdot5^4\mid n$$

$$n = \text{lcm}(3^2,\ 7^5,\ 2^2\cdot5^4) = 2^2\cdot3^2\cdot5^4\cdot7^5$$

$$\text{Number of divisors} = (2+1)(2+1)(4+1)(5+1) = 270$$

$$\textbf{Question}$$

$$\text{A } 3\times3 \text{ array contains digits 1 through 9, increasing along every row and column.}$$

$$\text{How many such arrays are there?}$$
problems.solutionText:
$$\textbf{Solution (Hook Length Formula)}$$

$$\text{Hook lengths for a } 3\times3 \text{ grid:}$$

$$\begin{matrix}5&4&3\\4&3&2\\3&2&1\end{matrix}$$

$$f = \frac{9!}{5\cdot4\cdot3\cdot4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1} = \frac{362880}{8640} = 42$$

problems.questionText:
$$\textbf{Question}$$

$$\text{Find all integers } x \text{ such that } x^2+5x+3 \text{ is a perfect square}$$
problems.solutionText:
$$\textbf{Solution}$$

$$\text{For } x>1: \quad (x+2)^2 < x^2+5x+3 < (x+3)^2$$

$$\text{No perfect square lies strictly between consecutive squares, so no solutions for } x\geq2$$

$$\text{For } x<-6: \quad (x-3)^2 < x^2+5x+3 < (x-2)^2 \quad \text{(same contradiction)}$$

$$\text{Check remaining } -6\leq x\leq1 \text{ directly:}$$

$$x=1: \ 1+5+3=9=3^2 \ \checkmark \qquad x=-6: \ 36-30+3=9=3^2 \ \checkmark$$

$$\text{All other values in this range give non-squares}$$

$$x=1 \quad \text{or} \quad x=-6$$

problems.questionText:
$$\textbf{Question}$$

$$\text{How many roots of } z^{12}=1 \text{ have } z^4 \text{ real?}$$
problems.solutionText:
$$\textbf{Solution}$$

$$z = e^{i\frac{2\pi k}{12}}, \quad k=0,1,\ldots,11$$

$$z^4 = e^{i\frac{2\pi k}{3}}$$

$$\text{Real when } \frac{2k}{3} \in \mathbb{Z} \implies k \equiv 0 \pmod 3$$

$$k=0,3,6,9 \implies \text{4 roots}$$
